citations.quote: BOREALIS is a 6U CubeSat mission funded by the Italian Space Agency within the ALCOR programme and being developed by Bologna University, the School of Aerospace Engineering of Sapienza University of Rome and Kayser Italia Srl. In this paper, we implement model-based systems engineering on the 6U CubeSat concept design and select appropriate mission profiles to pursue the project objectives.
The primary scientific goal of BOREALIS is to assess the combined impact of microgravity and ionizing radiation onto the growth and evolution of genetically modified microbial biofilms.

To achieve this goal, the BOREALIS CubeSat will be deployed in LEO, where the shielding by the geomagnetic field leads to a dominant effect of microgravity and will be later transferred to a MEO of altitude of 2000 km, enabling an extensive examination of the effects of increased radiation exposure.

In particular, model-based systems engineering (MBSE) was implemented for the preliminary selection the on-board subsystems and devices, defining the concept design of the satellite platform. MBSE was integrated with the results obtained using the General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) by NASA to simulate mission profiles associated with different types of propulsion systems. The analysis also led to the definition of the acceptable altitude for the deployment orbit (LEO) and transfer time (LEO-MEO). Moreover, the dose rates estimated by numerical simulations for different orbits allowed computing the total ionizing dose (TID).

Flight data collected during ABCS mission proved that both the payload and supporting devices (i.e. sealed box and shield) operated correctly and the dose rate estimation and flight firmware programmer development were also appropriate, ensuring satellite operation under nominal conditions [14].
The ABCS mission provided pivotal information to develop the BOREALIS satellite platform, embarking a similar primary payload and shields [14].

MBSE is implemented for BOREALIS to use numerical tools, such as the browser-based software Valispace, that turn MBSE into Data-driven systems engineering (DDSE) through linking requirements and components with engineering data (budgets of power, mass, volume, storage, etc.)

Thus, Valispace has been used for BOREALIS to design the 6U CubeSat system model, link the scientific, system and subsystem requirements, conduct the concurrent engineering by sharing the data and informing team members about the system and subsystems changes, and finally checking for
any interference of the system between the subsystems mass, power, volume and dimensions.

to distinguish the effects associated with microgravity and cosmic radiation, the satellite will have to operate for a relevant amount of time (enough to perform the experiments and collect data) on orbits in which the intensity of the cosmic radiation is significantly different
the deployment orbit must be compatible with the rideshare performance of Vega-C (and eventually other launch vehicles)
within 5 years from the end of the mission, the satellite will no longer have to orbit in LEO (below 2000 km)
the TID collected during the operative mission will be limited to ensure the survival of the microbial cultures and the operativity of onboard devices and subsystems

A study dedicated to estimating the dose rate for BOREALIS suggests that the satellite must be released at an altitude of less than 1200 km and then raised to an altitude of 2000 km (or more) in order to satisfy the specification (1) [19].

citations.quote: The BOREALIS mission employs a MBSE approach throughout its development lifecycle with the support of a specific software platform (Valispace) and some dedicated data sheets for first iterations and initial budgeting. This approach starts with an analysis of constraints and requirements, progressing through systematic model development, to final system realization. MBSE helps in visualizing, analysing, and managing the complexities of system design, particularly beneficial in the intricate environment of space missions.

All the BOREALIS system is based on the payload specifications and on the requirements of the mission analysis, specifically on the two target orbits and the consequences they have mainly on the propulsion system choice. Volume and mass of the propulsion system is one of the key driver of the system design, since such a large orbit transfer has hardly been performed with CubeSats platform. This is then one of the main challenges of BOREALIS mission design and execution. After the definition of these key system elements, all the other main subsystem choices have been designed around, including Electric Power System (EPS), Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) sensors and actuators, communication system, On-Board Computer (OBC), and Thermal Control System (TCS).

As a general System Engineering approach, a first analysis on scientific requirements and the identification of mission constraints has been conducted. Starting from its result, the degrees of freedom of the system have been identified as architectural decisions (ADs) for the BOREALIS 6U CubeSat. These are reported in Table 9. Starting from the combinations of the different options for each architectural decisions different mission concepts were generated. Nine (9) of these concepts were selected and reported in the table shown in Figure 3 for a quantitative analysis, to evaluate their performance in the context of BOREALIS mission objectives.
AD1, Primary Power Source: Option 1 Body-mounted solar array; Option 2 Large deployable solar array; Option 3 Deployable solar array + Large batteries.

A yellow triangle denotes the utopia point, representing the ideal mission with maximum utility and minimum cost. Quantitative analyses on the model output, including Monte Carlo simulations and sensitivity analysis on the variable's weights, were conducted to include uncertainty in the model output and verify if any concept changed its relative utility and cost with respect to the others. The results are reported in the following tradespace as a summary.
Concept 8 (HPGP+RT Proc) uses a body-mounted solar array and mono-propellant HPGP. Concept 10 (HET+RT Proc) uses a deployable solar array and a Hall-effect thruster.

citations.quote: The tradespace analysis plots MAU against cost for each concept, ultimately leading to the selection of Concept 10 (HET+RT Proc). This concept features a particular electric propulsion unit which is a balance between the critical propulsion volume and mass constraints and the transfer time which is typically increased using this class of propulsion units. At a first stage, Concept 8 (HPGP+RT Proc) was considered to be the most suitable as baseline. This concept, featuring body-mounted solar arrays, UHF and S-band transceivers, a mono-propellant HPGP system, and realtime data processing, offered the best balance between high utility and manageable cost, ensuring the mission's scientific and operational success. With a second iteration, having verified the availability of HET propulsors with compatible TRL on the market, concept 10 has been introduced in the model and it presented better performance as showed in Figure 5.

In addition, a Monte Carlo analysis has been performed (see Figure 6) to account for the data variability and check for the relative performance of the concepts. In addition, a sensitivity analysis on each weight has also been performed by varying all of them of 30% obtaining the same results.

In the graphs, it is reported the utopia point which is the ideal case of maximum utility at minimum cost; in addition, the Pareto front indicates the level of the most efficient concepts among which the optimal solution is then chosen, note that since concept 10 has been added in a second iteration it has not been included in the former Pareto front to clearly show its superior performance.

citations.quote: The BOREALIS CubeSat implemented MBSE with the support of Valispace, Monte Carlo analysis to select the best concept and model among the presented ones with the specific variables of utility and cost, conducted mission analysis for its specific LEO-MEO mission requirements, propulsion selected regarding mission performance and TID accumulation considering the needed propellent mass and volume.

Through the presented comprehensive system analysis, including the exploration of alternative mission concepts and the incorporation of a MBSE provided insightful results defining a preliminary mission baseline concept.

The system engineering approach and tools used in this first part of the mission have been presented with detail, including the trade-space analysis and the additional quantitative analysis used to validate the model (Monte Carlo and sensitivity analysis).

The next steps will involve implementing the detailed design of all the subsystems, procurement activities of the main parts, payload manufacturing and testing, and maintaining close collaboration with stakeholders to ensure the mission's continued success.

MBSE also promotes better collaboration and communication among team members by offering a unified language and system representation, which is especially useful for large, complex systems with many stakeholders. Additionally, MBSE incorporates computer-aided tools and techniques to enhance the design process, whereas traditional methods often rely on manual calculations and drawings.
